tier_reason: The README Performance section gives a table from benches/bench_multiprocess/src/main.rs. It has OpenSSL SHA-1 (3.51 cpb) and SHA-512 (5.11 cpb) rows next to blake2b_simd BLAKE2b (2.81), many::hash (1.43) and BLAKE2bp (1.44), and states rustc 1.40.0, clang 9.0.1, `cargo run --release` and an Intel Core i5-8250U. Public code, compiler, build mode and CPU model are all present, so tier A holds.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.40.0, `cargo run --release` (default release profile with no target-cpu flag; the crate picks SIMD paths by runtime CPU-feature detection). clang 9.0.1 was used only for Samuel Neves' blake2-avx2 C reference, built with `-mavx2` in benches/blake2-avx2-sneves/build.rs. OpenSSL 1.1.1d and libsodium 1.0.18 were linked through the openssl and libsodium-ffi crates, and the build flags of those libraries are not stated.
corrections.workload: 1,000,000-byte in-memory inputs hashed by BLAKE3, blake2b_simd/blake2s_simd (single, many::hash, BLAKE2bp/BLAKE2sp), libsodium BLAKE2b and OpenSSL SHA-1/SHA-512. Each algorithm runs in 100 worker processes across all 512 input offsets. Total time is averaged (a mean, not a median) and reported as cycles per byte (benches/bench_multiprocess).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 144 stars; crates.io: blake2b_simd ~57.8M downloads, blake2s_simd ~23.0M downloads
corrections.caveats: The numbers were last updated in the README on 2020-01-30 (rustc 1.40, OpenSSL 1.1.1d, libsodium 1.0.18) and come from one laptop. The bench crate has since been updated (edition 2024, blake3 1.8.3), so a rerun today uses different code and toolchains. The main comparison crosses algorithms. BLAKE2b, BLAKE2bp and many::hash are not drop-in replacements for SHA-512/SHA-1, since they produce different digests, and BLAKE2bp is a separate parallel mode. Against the same algorithm (libsodium BLAKE2b, 3.07 cpb), the win is only ~1.09x (derived from page data). The i5-8250U has no SHA-NI, so OpenSSL SHA-1 ran without hardware SHA extensions, and the margin would be smaller on SHA-NI CPUs. The bench code measures nanoseconds, and the README does not say how it converted them to cpb. Only first-party runs on a single machine exist.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup matches the README table exactly, and the derived ratios are correct (5.11/2.81 = 1.82x, 5.11/1.43-1.44 = 3.55-3.57x, 3.51/1.43-1.44 = 2.44-2.45x). The repo is active (v1.0.5 on 2026-08-20 removed the compromised arrayref dependency), MIT, not a fork, and widely used on crates.io. I corrected the record's claim about what clang built and changed 'median' to 'mean'.

tier_reason: benchmark_example.md tables the repo's C-intrinsic SHA-256/SHA-512 against OpenSSL's x86-64 assembly (avx/avx2/sha-ext 'ossl' columns) in cycles. The harness is tests/main_speed.c, which switches only the compression backend inside the same sha256()/sha512() wrapper. The page states clang-9 and an i7-1065G7 with Turbo off, and cmake/compilation-flags.cmake gives the flags (-O3 -march=native). Code, compiler, flags and CPU are all present, so tier A holds.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang-9, CMake Release build with TEST_SPEED. cmake/compilation-flags.cmake sets -O3 -march=native -mno-red-zone -fPIC -std=c99 -ggdb, not -O2. The OpenSSL .s files are assembled into the same binary. The repo was also built and tested with gcc-9.
corrections.baseline: OpenSSL SHA-256/SHA-512 x86-64 perlasm assembly (AVX and AVX2 paths, plus the SHA-NI path for SHA-256 only), copied into the repo from OpenSSL master as of Feb 24 2020 (README link text says 13c5d744, but the URL points to commit e32c608e)
corrections.workload: Full SHA-256/SHA-512 hashing through the same sha256()/sha512() wrapper, switching only the compression backend (C intrinsics vs OpenSSL asm), on message sizes from 1 to 65536 bytes. Each function gets 25 warm-up runs, then 100 timed iterations averaged, and each experiment is repeated 10 times with the minimum reported, in CPU cycles (tests/main_speed.c).
corrections.caveats: This is a mixed result. Only the SHA-256 SHA-NI C path beats OpenSSL: ~1.05-1.08x at 64 bytes and up (424 vs 446 cycles at 64 B, 183,685 vs 198,528 at 65536 B), and it ties at 32 bytes or less (281 vs 280 at 32 B, derived from page data). Every AVX/AVX2 C path, and all of SHA-512 (which has no SHA-NI path), loses to OpenSSL's asm, e.g. SHA-512 avx2 456,221 vs 402,204 cycles at 65536 B. The authors frame the repo as compiler feedback: they say C built with gcc-9/clang-9 'is often slower than the performance of hand written assembly code'. It ships only test binaries, with no shared or static library, and is 'designed to be used for benchmarking purposes only and not in final products'. The numbers are from 2020, against an unreleased OpenSSL master snapshot, on one Ice Lake laptop built with -march=native. The repo has had a single commit (2020-05-31) and is abandoned. The authors are Drucker & Gueron (AWS Crypto Algorithms Group).

notes: The numbers match the page exactly. The ~8% SHA-NI win is real but narrow, and the authors themselves say C intrinsics are generally slower than asm and that the code is not for production. Treat this as a borderline entry: keep it only if single-path wins of ~5-8% qualify. Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 21 stars, not archived or forked, last commit 2020-05-31.
